query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (approximately 2–5 at.%) of Hf to refractory high-entropy alloys promotes the in situ formation of fine, stable precipitates (such as carbides or oxides) during subsequent heat treatments that strengthen the alloy without compromising its thermal or irradiation stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) exhibiting a single-phase BCC (or similarly stable) structure achieved via conventional processing (e.g., rolling and recrystallization).
generation.intervention: Incorporate 2–5 atomic percent Hf into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: Followed by standard post-processing heat treatments at temperatures typical for in-service operation (e.g., 1000–1200 °C) and performance evaluation under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dispersion of fine Hf-containing precipitates (e.g., Hf carbides or oxides) that reside along grain boundaries and within grains.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and defect migration, increasing yield strength while also impeding the evolution of irradiation-induced defects. Their presence stabilizes grain structures during high-temperature exposure by pinning grain boundaries and reducing coarsening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an undoped baseline alloy, the Hf-doped alloy will show enhanced yield strength and hardness without a reduction in high-temperature and irradiation stability. Ductility may remain comparable provided the precipitate size and distribution are well controlled.
generation.baseline: Refractory HEA processed under the same conditions without Hf doping.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected when Hf additions are maintained within the 2–5 at.% range and when processing parameters (e.g., heat-treatment temperature and time) favor fine precipitate formation; deviations in concentration or processing may lead to undesirable phase segregation or overcoarsening that could undermine the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties and the long-term stability under irradiation are uncertain and may depend on the exact processing route and interactions with other alloying elements. Potential risks such as embrittlement due to coarsened precipitates at higher Hf levels must be considered.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with 2–5 at.% Hf doping and one as the undoped control. Process both sets identically with rolling and recrystallization, then subject them to the same heat treatment to induce precipitate formation. Evaluate the samples under high-temperature conditions and expose them to controlled ion irradiation.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and phase stability.
Mechanical tests (nanoindentation, tensile testing) to determine yield strength, hardness, and ductility pre- and post-irradiation.
Irradiation damage assessment (e.g., defect density via TEM) after controlled irradiation fluences.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength/hardness or if they show a degradation in thermal or irradiation stability (e.g., excessive precipitate coarsening, phase transformation, or increased irradiation-induced defect density) relative to the undoped control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Beside the contained elements in HEA, doping with interstitial elements such as carbon to HEA has been announced to be an effective way to improve the mechanical properties [,,,,,,,]. The tensile yield strength of CoCrFeMnNi could increase from 371 MPa to 792 MPa just by adding 3.0 at.% C []. It was reported that the doped C atoms may have strong interactions with elements in HEA to form carbides, which usually lead to higher strength. As expected, both the yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength increase with the carbon content increasing in CoCrFeMnNi []. By analogy, the increase of both compressive strength and the plasticity of the Mo0.5NbHf0.5ZrTi refractory HEA (RHEA) was attributed to the formation of carbides (MC with M = Nb, Hf, Zr, and Ti), when the concertation of C was only 0.3 at.%, a dilute doping case [].

Often, the strengthening effect due to the formation of oxides and carbides is followed by a decrease in ductility []. It is also possible that more carbon was introduced to the powder during milling, due to the wear of the milling jar and balls. This is possibly caused by the high carbon content of the milling jar (1.5 wt.%) and milling balls (1 wt.%). While it simply precipitates as carbides during sintering, more milling appears to lead to more carbide formation. It seems that the formation of zirconium carbide is the most thermodynamically favorable in the given system and used conditions, pertaining to its highest stability, with respect to other possible carbides of other elements.
